results.title: Selective persistence of HIV-1-infected T cell clones can occur through immune reprogramming driven by defective, transcriptionally active proviruses.
results.authorString: Hamann MV, Brauckmann L, Schwarz C, Spohn M, Stoeck R, Leddy SM, Frouard J, Adiba M, Winzer R, Hausmann F, Virdi S, Grundhoff A, Feschotte C, Sauter D, Muecksch F, Roan NR, Tolosa E, Lange UC.
results.abstractText: People living with HIV (PLWH) on antiretroviral therapy (ART) accumulate primarily defective proviral sequences in genomes of often clonally expanded CD4 + HIV-1 target cells. The majority of viral-derived DNA is transcriptionally active and preferentially found at distinct genomic loci suggesting a selective process driven by integration site-specific crosstalk between viral and host sequences. Focusing on one of the most prominent selected integration loci, the BTB Domain and CNC Homolog 2 (BACH2) gene, we here show mechanistic insights how CD4 + T cells are functionally reprogrammed via exaptation of provirus-derived regulatory sequences during long-term ART. Using a cellular model of BACH2-integrated proviruses, we find that proviral transcription drives aberrant BACH2 protein levels that escape autoregulatory feedback and impose BACH2-dependent transcriptomic changes. By mimicking these changes in primary CD4 + T lymphocytes, we observe that BACH2 drives reprogramming of cells toward a proliferative, precursor memory-like type. These reprogrammed CD4 + T cells possess traits of immune evasion and cellular survival that are signatures of persistent HIV reservoir cells in PLWH. Inhibition of provirus transcriptional activity can mitigate exaptation, suggesting a strategy to offset HIV-driven differentiation and expansion of CD4 + T cells. Finally, our data suggest that provirus exaptation at a second prominently selected proviral integration gene, the Signal Transducer And Activator of Transcription 5B (STAT5B) gene, drives a contrary, effector-like T cell fate, suggesting a multifaceted impact of exaptation on immune homeostasis. Overall, our data suggest that transcriptionally active proviruses, even if structurally defective, modulate target cells through insertional activation of integration genes, a process which we postulate to contribute to the complex immune modulation and dysregulation experienced by ART-suppressed PLWH.

results.title: Characterization of therapeutic antibodies targeting lymphatic and vascular resistance factor for the treatment of hypervascularized and highly metastatic cancers.
results.authorString: David M, Karaulic A, Bennetot A, Fournier C, Odet Q, Gouraud A, Bourget I, Gaggioli C, Giuliano S, Luciano F, Léger O, Sellam Z, Pagès G.
results.abstractText: Angiogenesis is a major driver of tumor progression and a validated therapeutic target in highly vascularized cancers such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma. However, the clinical benefit of antivascular endothelial growth factor therapies is limited by the emergence of resistance. We identified a vascular endothelial growth factor A splice variant, termed Lymphatic and Vascular Resistance Factor (LVRF), which promotes both angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis and is upregulated following anti-angiogenic treatment. To therapeutically target this pathway, we generated fully human monoclonal antibodies against LVRF. Lead antibodies displayed high specificity and nanomolar affinity and effectively inhibited LVRF-driven biological activities. Anti-LVRF antibodies reduced renal carcinoma cell invasion, inhibited vascular and lymphatic endothelial responses, and suppressed lymphatic endothelial cell sprouting. In vivo, treatment significantly reduced the growth of bevacizumab-resistant renal carcinoma xenografts, induced regression of blood and lymphatic vessels, and decreased metastatic dissemination in zebrafish models. These findings identify LVRF as a mediator of resistance to anti-angiogenic therapy and support therapeutic targeting of LVRF as a novel strategy for vascularized tumors resistant to current antivascular endothelial growth factor treatments.

results.title: Dysregulated AKT signaling reprograms osteosarcoma to drive selective reliance on EP300.
results.authorString: Delahunty IM, Nance S, Zhang Y, Lamoureux F, Liu Q, Wright WC, Ritter KE, Shendy NAM, Brounais-Le Roye B, Kietlinska SJ, Mohammad Nezhady MA, Feng Y, De Kegel B, Rees MG, Kocak M, George AB, Lu M, Kavirayani AM, Wang B, Liu Y, Prinsen PEA, Khashana Y, Ebegboni VJ, Ronan MM, Roth JA, Sweet-Cordero EA, Guenther LM, Geeleher P, Ma X, Ory B, Qi J, Abraham BJ, Durbin AD.
results.abstractText: Cancers depend on transcriptional control to maintain the malignant cell state. EP300 and CBP are paralogous master epigenetic enzymes that control normal and malignant transcription. Using a cancer-wide integrative chemical-genetic analysis, we demonstrate enhanced dependency on EP300, compared with CBP, in cell lines from most cancer lineages, including lethal osteosarcoma (OS). Using a selective EP300 degrader (JQAD1), we identify that a genetically defined subgroup of OS with dysregulation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway is genetically and chemically sensitive to loss of EP300. Activated AKT promotes sensitivity to JQAD1, driven by relocalization of EP300, CBP and H3K27ac to genetic subtype-enriched dependency loci. AKT inhibition combines with JQAD1 to synergistically suppress the growth of AKT-dysregulated OS cells in vitro and in orthotopic xenografts. These observations extend across >850 cancer cell lines, where synergy is predicted by elevated protein synthetic rates. These findings reveal determinants of EP300 degrader function in OS and provide a foundation for co-targeting EP300 and AKT in cancers with enhanced protein translation.

results.title: An integrated human forebrain organoid reveals microglia-mediated CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell recruitment and neuroimmune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease pathology.
results.authorString: Feng Y, Yu F, Tang J, Zheng H, Wang Z, Ma S.
results.abstractText: Genetic evidence implicates immune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the neuroimmune mechanisms operating in human tissue remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a modular human forebrain organoid platform that systematically integrates human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells to reconstitute multicellular AD pathology. This system enables functional interrogation of both innate and adaptive immune components in a human-relevant context. Using this platform, we demonstrate that microglia mediate amyloid-β clearance and neuronal maturation but also drive inflammatory activation and recruit CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells through CCL4/5 signaling via CCR1/5 and CXCR3, establishing a neuroinflammatory feedback loop. Pharmacological targeting of CCR5 or CXCR3 blocks T cell recruitment and modulates autophagy in a microglia-dependent manner. This modular organoid platform provides a versatile tool for dissecting neuron-immune interactions and enables cell-type-specific therapeutic screening in human neuroinflammatory disease models.

results.title: Matrix metalloproteinase-guided targeting of vesicular stomatitis virus to tumors following systemic administration.
results.authorString: Theune EV, Theune WC, Ahmadi E, Chiari CC, Singh N, Geyer R, Tonne J, Metko M, Olaoba OT, Wang IC, Dai D, Ruan J, Clark R, Li G, Wang P, Jellison ER, Vella AT, Vile R, Wang K.
results.abstractText: The lack of tumor-specific targeting by oncolytic viruses (OVs) restricts their therapeutic potential. Here, we report a "cap-linker" strategy to modify the vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) glycoprotein (G protein, VSV-G<sup>IN</sup>). The modified VSV (Pro-VSV<sup>IN</sup>) loses its ability to infect cells until present in the tumor microenvironment, where the linker is cleaved by tumor-enriched matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). When Pro-VSV<sup>IN</sup> is armed with a single-chain IL-12 (Pro-VSV<sup>IN</sup>-IL-12) and systemically injected into MC38 tumor-bearing mice, Pro-VSV<sup>IN</sup>-IL-12 eradicates established tumors while avoiding systemic toxicity, and elicits long-term anti-tumor immune memory. Systemic administration of Pro-VSV<sup>IN</sup>-IL-12 also markedly inhibits the growth of metastatic cancers in the lung. The efficacy of Pro-VSV<sup>IN</sup>-IL-12 was further improved when combined with PD-1 checkpoint blockade. Compared to WT VSV<sup>IN</sup> that carries IL-12, intravenously injected Pro-VSV<sup>IN</sup>-IL-12 leads to strong Th1 immunity, near abolishment of regulatory T cells, and potent CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell activation and clonal expansion in tumors. This preclinical work demonstrates a new tumor-specific targeting strategy of VSV for enhanced immunotherapy safety with superior efficacy.
